v: Go get RAJINIfied!!! Karthik Subbaraj finally gives the Superstar a much-needed commercial potboiler, with Rajini’s style and Anirudh’s terrific BGM doing exactly what fans came for.
e: Petta is not trying to win anyone with airtight logic or a fresh story; it is designed to celebrate Rajinikanth’s screen presence after a run of slower, message-heavy films. Karthik Subbaraj understands that brief, Anirudh gives the mass moments a superb canvas, and Vijay Sethupathi, Nawazuddin Siddiqui and Simran add extra flavour.
body:
Go get RAJINIfied!!!

After the social-message-oriented, slower films Rajinikanth had been doing with Pa. Ranjith, Karthik Subbaraj finally delivers the kind of commercial potboiler the Superstar badly needed 🙏

And because this is unapologetically a commercial Rajini movie, I am not going to spend much time worrying about logic or the basic storyline.

The real job here is to glorify Rajini’s screen presence and style — and Karthik does that successfully.

Anirudh’s BGM is terrific as usual and creates the perfect canvas for Rajini to unleash that seemingly never-ending stylish charisma.

The film also slips in a few cheeky political digs along the way, which I enjoyed 😛

Vijay Sethupathi and Nawazuddin Siddiqui do not get the meatiest roles of their careers, but both still become icing on the cake simply because of the quality they bring to the screen.

And after a long gap, it was genuinely pleasant to see Simran back on the big screen.

She looks beautiful, and the little romantic portions between her and Rajini are handled very sweetly.

Rajini’s very first dialogue carries the line, “Ayipoyanu anukunaru kadharaaaaaaa…” followed by that trademark laugh.

It almost feels intentionally written for the star himself.

His career may have gone through a low phase, but Petta is a reminder that he is never completely out of the race!!!!!

v: DISAPPOINTED!!! This material needed the breathing room of a multi-season web series, not a three-hour parade of familiar movie moments. Balayya gives 1000%, but the film lacks depth for a wider audience.
e: NTR: Kathanayakudu works best for viewers who simply want to relive NTR’s charisma and revisit famous incidents from his film career. For me, the lack of dramatic setbacks, the endless recreations and the difficulty of accepting Balakrishna as a much younger NTR make the three-hour film feel shallow despite his enormous effort and a few excellent scenes.
body:
DISAPPOINTED!!!

I honestly think this story could have worked much better as a multi-season web series rather than a single movie.

When I watch a biopic, I broadly see three kinds of audiences.

One group wants to relive the charisma of the person.

Another wants to understand the ups and downs of that life and how the person overcame challenges.

And a third group does not care about either — they simply want a good movie.

Mahanati became such a classic for me because it had enough content to satisfy all three groups.

NTR: Kathanayakudu struggles badly with that balance.

After NTR’s initial period of struggle, there are simply not enough failures or major dramatic conflicts in this portion of his life to sustain three hours of cinema.

There are four or five scenes that genuinely elevate the drama, but that is too little to carry such a long film.

There is also the obvious challenge of Balakrishna playing his own father across different ages.

It is relatively easy to make a younger actor look older with makeup.

Doing the reverse is much harder.

For me, it was difficult to accept Balayya as a young man beginning his journey and chasing his dreams.

That said, Balakrishna puts in 1000% effort to make the film memorable for his family, party and hardcore NTR fans.

The problem is not the commitment; it is that the movie itself never develops enough depth to reach a much larger audience.

The Mayabazar/Lord Krishna recreation is excellently shot.

On the other hand, the self-congratulatory moments around Balayya himself could easily have been avoided.

The later part of the second half finally becomes engaging, but by then I was already exhausted by the endless movie recreations 😦

Watch it mainly for Balayya and for a high-level visual recap of stories and incidents many of us already know.

I only hoped the next part, Mahanayakudu, would offer more drama for all three kinds of audiences.

v: Give 2.0 its due credit! Shankar’s out-of-the-box sci-fi concept, top-notch visualisation and world-class Rahman BGM prove why Indian cinema needs creators willing to dream this BIG.
e: 2.0 worked for me as a focused futuristic sci-fi film rather than a regular star vehicle. Shankar builds the entire movie around one unusual idea, keeps commercial distractions to a minimum and pushes Indian visual effects towards an ambitious scale, while A.R. Rahman’s BGM and the final Rajini-heavy stretch deliver the spectacle.
body:
I had seen plenty of posts either celebrating or mocking 2.0’s collections, but for me the larger point was much simpler.

If a film this ambitious fails purely because audiences refuse to support the experiment, Indian cinema risks losing creators with the imagination of Shankar.

How on earth does this man keep coming up with such out-of-the-box concepts and visual ideas? 🙏

Like a big Hollywood genre film, 2.0 revolves around one central concept and avoids stuffing the screenplay with unnecessary commercial distractions.

Shankar’s visualisation is top-notch.

The scale of what he imagines also makes the CGI team’s job incredibly difficult, and throughout the movie you can sense the challenge of turning those drawings and ideas into convincing imagery.

Story-wise, one aspect I particularly loved is the decision to look at the human race itself from a negative angle.

After Avatar, I had rarely seen a mainstream spectacle take that kind of position so directly.

A.R. Rahman’s BGM is world class.

Rajini fans need to wait until roughly the final thirty minutes to get the full blast of trademark Superstar style, but when that stretch arrives the film knows exactly how to use him.

I can only wonder what Shankar might have achieved if the visual-effects process had been smoother and given him every tool he originally imagined.

And I do not think comparing this film mechanically with Baahubali makes much sense.

Baahubali is a grand period drama built on a familiar revenge foundation and packaged brilliantly by Rajamouli.

2.0 is a futuristic science-fiction film attempting a completely different kind of story and technical challenge.

Both deserve to be judged for what they are trying to achieve.

Shankar has repeatedly shown that he wants to build films around unusual ideas — whether it is I or this story about our dependence on mobile technology turning against humanity.

Give that creative ambition its due credit.

v: Neither great nor bad — just a good time-pass movie. Nani handles the acting, Nag handles the glamour 😄 and their chemistry rescues a very basic story and execution.
e: Deva Das has an ordinary plot and equally basic execution, but its casting changes the experience considerably. Nani’s effortless expressions and Nagarjuna’s screen presence give the film most of its charm, while an impressive BGM and regular laughs make it an easy time-pass watch if you leave the logical brain at home.
body:
Deva Das has a normal, basic storyline and equally basic execution.

You never feel as though you are watching a great movie, but you do not really feel as though you are watching a bad movie either.

The director tries to balance commercial entertainment with a message-oriented angle, and the biggest strength of that attempt is the casting.

The film understands how to use Nani’s natural acting ability and Nagarjuna’s superb screen presence, and that combination becomes the real game changer.

Coming to Nani… man, what an actor!!!!!

He makes everything look easy with those wonderfully natural and cute expressions 🙏

And then there is Nag.

His screen presence alone is enough in many scenes, and his fitness and handsome levels are outstanding.

It almost feels as though while Nani was busy handling the acting department, Nagarjuna took responsibility for the movie’s glamour department 😄

The heroines unfortunately do not get much to work with.

The songs are again average — almost every number sits in that neither-good-nor-bad zone.

The BGM, however, is quite impressive and gives the movie more energy than the soundtrack.

Overall, it is a good time-pass movie with regular laughs every few minutes, provided you are willing to keep the logical part of your brain comfortably at home.
